title: Apple Just Agreed to Hand Over Its India Financials to the Antitrust Regulator. It Had Refused for Years.
excerpt: The CCI found Apple abused its dominant position in 2024. Apple fought the case and withheld its books. A Delhi judge told the company to cooperate. Now it has.
body:
Apple has agreed to submit the financial details of its India business to the Competition Commission of India, a capitulation that takes a four-year-old antitrust case significantly closer to a penalty decision. The reversal, first reported by Reuters, could expose the company to a fine calculated on its India revenue — and possibly much more.

A confidential CCI order reviewed by Reuters showed that Apple's lawyer requested a "final extension" until June 25 to file India-specific financial information at a hearing on May 21. The commission granted the request. The document marked a decisive shift: for years, Apple had refused to provide financial details to the regulator, arguing that the entire proceeding should be paused.

How the case began

The investigation traces back to 2021, when a coalition of complainants including Match Group, the parent company of Tinder, and the Alliance of Digital India Foundation, which represents Indian startups, filed complaints about Apple's App Store policies. The specific allegation: Apple forced developers to use its in-app payment system exclusively, extracting commissions of up to 30 percent while blocking alternative payment channels.

The CCI's investigation concluded in 2024. Its finding was unambiguous — Apple had abused its dominant position in the market for iPhone apps. The App Store, the CCI said, was "an unavoidable trading partner" for any developer seeking to reach India's growing base of iPhone users.

Apple denied wrongdoing and said it would contest the findings.

The financial standoff

What turned the case into a prolonged standoff was money — specifically, how much of it the CCI could access when calculating a potential fine.

India's revised antitrust penalty law empowers the CCI to levy fines based on a company's global revenue, not just domestic earnings. Apple argued this provision was unconstitutional and filed a parallel challenge in court, insisting the CCI case should be frozen until the legal question was resolved. The stakes were staggering: under the global-revenue framework, Apple's maximum exposure could reach $38 billion.

The CCI repeatedly rejected Apple's position, pointing out that it was only requesting India-specific financials to begin with. The regulator accused Apple of using the parallel court challenge as a delay tactic.

Last month, a Delhi High Court judge directed Apple to cooperate with the investigation. Apple complied.

India is too important to fight

The timing of Apple's reversal is not accidental. India has become Apple's most consequential growth market outside the United States. The iPhone's market share in India has climbed from roughly 2 percent five years ago to 9 percent today, according to Counterpoint Research. Apple has rapidly expanded iPhone production in the country as it diversifies its manufacturing base away from China, and the Indian smartphone market — the world's second largest — is one of the few places where Apple still has room to grow.

Picking a prolonged regulatory fight with the Indian government, at a moment when the government is simultaneously facilitating Apple's manufacturing expansion, carries risks that extend well beyond any single fine.

What happens next

Apple has until June 25 to submit its India financial data. Once the CCI has the numbers, it can proceed to calculate a penalty — if it decides to impose one. The Alliance of Digital India Foundation has urged the commission to move quickly and avoid further delays.

The case mirrors regulatory battles Apple is fighting globally, from the European Union's Digital Markets Act to South Korea's app store payment rules. But India's combination of a large, fast-growing market and an assertive competition regulator makes it a jurisdiction Apple cannot afford to alienate.

For India's startup ecosystem, the outcome will set a precedent for how dominant global platforms operate in the country. If the CCI imposes a meaningful penalty, it will send a signal that India's antitrust framework has teeth — and that even Apple must comply.
